analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to buy cheaper prescription drugs from Canada through certified pharmacies and wholesalers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to allow pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals to import prescription drugs from licensed Canadian sellers, and later from other countries with comparable safety standards. It included safety rules — seller certification, drug testing, recall requirements — and penalties for drug makers that tried to block the flow of cheaper medicine into the US. It was introduced by Rep. Elijah Cummings with 29 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs — especially the uninsured and people with high out-of-pocket costs — would be able to buy the same medicines from certified Canadian sellers at Canadian prices, sometimes far lower. US pharmacies and wholesalers could also import cheaper stock.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high US drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the FDA to write rules within 180 days letting wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals import qualifying prescription drugs from licensed Canadian sellers, giving Americans access to the same medicines at Canada's lower prices.

Individuals could buy up to a 90-day personal supply directly from a certified Canadian pharmacy with a valid US prescription, an option aimed especially at people paying out of pocket for expensive drugs like insulin.

The bill included safety measures: foreign sellers had to be certified, pass quality testing including blind testing, and comply with recall requirements, and manufacturers were barred from deliberately limiting Canadian supply or making US-only versions of a drug to defeat importation.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to charge Americans more than Canadians pay for the same drugs, and could face restrictions on limiting supply or creating US-only versions of a drug to defeat importation. Insurers and employers would also see part of their drug costs fall.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs would bypass the US distribution system, and even with certification, testing, and tracing requirements, opponents argued in general that foreign channels raise the risk of counterfeit or substandard medicine reaching patients.

Drugmakers could be expected to respond by restricting or raising prices for Canadian supply — the bill makes such discrimination unlawful, but enforcing that against multinational manufacturers would be difficult, so the promised savings might partly fail to materialize.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — cheaper medicine for Americans who pay among the highest drug prices in the world — was potentially large and immediate, since Canadian prices for the same drugs are often far lower. The main cost, a small added risk of unsafe or counterfeit drugs slipping through, was addressed in the bill itself through seller certification, laboratory testing, and recall requirements, though no safeguard can reduce that risk to zero. The bill never got a vote, so the trade-off was never weighed by the full Congress; the costs of inaction — continued high drug prices — fell entirely on patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on February 28, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Five days later it was referred to the subcommittee on Health, which is where the record ends — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill never advanced in the Senate either, and when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, it expired along with every other bill not passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the US market closed to cheaper Canadian prices, and Americans kept paying US prices for the same medicines.

for.name: Rep. Elijah Cummings
for.role: Sponsor, House Oversight Committee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 original cosponsors from among House Democrats.

for.name: 29 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry has long campaigned against drug importation bills, arguing they would allow unsafe drugs; no industry opposition appears in this bill's congressional record.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over drug policy
against.what_they_did: The committee, to which the bill was referred, never held a hearing or markup, keeping the bill off the House floor for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to charge Americans more for the same drugs than Canadians pay, and would ban tactics like restricting Canadian supply or creating US-only drug versions to defeat importation. US patients currently pay substantially higher prices than patients in Canada.
They could gain a new, cheaper supply channel for importation, but would also face new price competition from Canadian sellers reaching American consumers directly.
They would become certified suppliers to a large new market of American customers, subject to certification fees, FDA testing, and compliance requirements.
